questions.stem: Which scientist discovered X-rays in 1895 and received the very first Nobel Prize in Physics (1901) for this achievement?

options.option_text: Marie Curie, famous for discovering polonium and radium
Wilhelm Röntgen, working at the University of Würzburg
Henri Becquerel, who studied natural uranium radioactivity
Max von Laue, known for X-ray diffraction through crystals

questions.explanation: Röntgen accidentally discovered X-rays while experimenting with cathode-ray tubes at Würzburg; he named them 'X' because their nature was unknown, and won Nobel Physics 1901. Marie Curie (Nobel 1903) discovered polonium and radium. Becquerel discovered uranium radioactivity. Von Laue (Nobel 1914) demonstrated X-ray diffraction but did not discover X-rays.

questions.stem: The movable-type printing press that enabled mass book production in Europe was invented around 1440 by:

options.option_text: William Caxton, who set up the first press in England
Aldus Manutius, who pioneered italic typeface in Venice
Johannes Gutenberg, the German goldsmith based in Mainz
Leonardo da Vinci, the Italian Renaissance polymath

questions.explanation: Gutenberg developed the movable-type press in Mainz (c. 1440), enabling the Gutenberg Bible (~1455) and revolutionising information spread. Caxton brought the press to England in 1476 — he adopted the technology, he did not invent it. Aldus Manutius was a 1490s Venetian publisher. Leonardo was an artist-engineer but had no role in press development.

questions.stem: The transistor, invented at Bell Labs in December 1947, transformed all modern electronics. Which team shared the Nobel Prize in Physics 1956 for this invention?

options.option_text: Bohr, Heisenberg, and Schrödinger (quantum physics founders)
Bardeen, Brattain, and Shockley (the Bell Labs research trio)
Fleming, Marconi, and de Forest (vacuum-tube technology pioneers)
Kilby, Noyce, and Moore (co-inventors of the integrated circuit)

questions.explanation: John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley demonstrated the point-contact transistor on 16 Dec 1947 and shared Nobel Physics 1956. Kilby and Noyce (not Moore) invented the integrated circuit. Fleming invented the vacuum diode; de Forest the triode — predecessors, not successors. Bohr/Heisenberg/Schrödinger provided theoretical foundations but did not invent the transistor.

questions.stem: The 1953 DNA double-helix model by Watson and Crick relied critically on unpublished X-ray data. Whose Photo 51 was the pivotal experimental evidence they used?

options.option_text: Erwin Chargaff, who established the A-T and G-C base-pairing rules
Rosalind Franklin, whose image directly revealed the helical form
Linus Pauling, who proposed an incorrect triple-helix structure
Maurice Wilkins, who later shared the Nobel Prize in 1962

questions.explanation: Photo 51 — taken by Rosalind Franklin in 1952 — unmistakably showed the B-form double helix. Watson viewed it without her knowledge via Wilkins. Chargaff's base-pairing ratios were essential but are not Photo 51. Maurice Wilkins did share the 1962 Nobel with Watson and Crick (Franklin had died by then), but Photo 51 was Franklin's work. Pauling proposed a wrong triple-helix model that spurred Watson and Crick to race ahead.

questions.stem: Which British physicist developed operational RADAR in the 1930s and built the Chain Home early-warning network that proved decisive during the Battle of Britain?

options.option_text: Guglielmo Marconi, Italian inventor of long-distance radio telegraphy
Nikola Tesla, who proposed radio-based detection concepts in the 1900s
Robert Watson-Watt, a Scottish physicist knighted for this work
Heinrich Hertz, who first experimentally produced electromagnetic waves

questions.explanation: Robert Watson-Watt demonstrated practical RADAR at Daventry (1935) and built Chain Home along Britain's coast (1937–40), giving the RAF advance warning of Luftwaffe raids. He received a knighthood in 1942. Marconi pioneered radio but not RADAR. Tesla conceptualised radio-wave detection but never built an operational system. Hertz (1887) demonstrated radio waves two decades before RADAR was conceived.

questions.stem: Dennis Gabor invented holography (Nobel Physics 1971) while trying to improve the resolution of an existing imaging device. Which device was he attempting to enhance?

options.option_text: The optical refracting telescope used in stellar astronomy
The X-ray crystallography camera at Bragg's Cavendish laboratory
The electron microscope, which suffered from severe lens aberrations
The cathode-ray oscilloscope used to visualise radio-wave signals

questions.explanation: Gabor conceived holography in 1947 at BTH Rugby precisely to overcome spherical aberration that blurred electron-microscope images. He used coherent light as an analogue to prove the wavefront-reconstruction principle, since lasers (needed for true electron holography) did not yet exist. The Nobel citation explicitly names the electron microscope problem. X-ray crystallography and radio oscilloscopes were unrelated to his motivation.

questions.stem: The CRISPR-Cas9 gene-editing mechanism (Nobel Chemistry 2020 to Charpentier and Doudna) was first observed functioning naturally in which type of organisms?

options.option_text: Plant cells of Arabidopsis thaliana in controlled laboratory studies
Yeast cells during experiments on fermentation enzyme pathways
Bacteria, where it serves as an adaptive immune defense against viruses
Archaea isolated from hypersaline lake-bed sediments in Spain

questions.explanation: CRISPR repeats were first reported in E. coli (Ishino et al., 1987) and the immune-defense function was confirmed in Streptococcus thermophilus bacteria (Barrangou et al., 2007). The Cas9 protein used in gene editing comes from Streptococcus pyogenes — a bacterium. Archaea also possess CRISPR loci, which is the key distractor, but bacteria were the original discovery site and primary functional characterisation. Yeast and plants lack Cas9-based CRISPR systems entirely.
